item.content:encoded:
Title for RSS: Agents that read shared rules, models that race on speed

Today’s builder news had one clear theme. People care less about “one more chat model.” They care about agents that follow shared project rules, and about models that are fast and cheap enough to use everywhere.

The biggest product move came from Claude Code. Thariq, who works on Claude Code at Anthropic, said version 2.1.277 now supports AGENTS.md. Here is the simple rule. If a folder has no CLAUDE.md, Claude will look for AGENTS.md and use it. You can turn this on or off in /config. That sounds small. It is not. Many open-source coding agents already use AGENTS.md as a shared place for project instructions. Claude Code catching up means one file can guide more tools in the same repo.

Thariq also explained the bigger plan. AGENTS.md support is built on Claude Code “mods.” Mods are Anthropic’s upcoming way to customize the Claude Code harness — the layer that wraps the model and steers how it works in your project. AGENTS.md is a built-in mod. Later, you will be able to build your own versions of project instructions. He also shared the mod’s source. So this is not only a checkbox. It is the start of a more open path for coding agents.

Speed was the other loud story, and the star was Jev. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said the adoption numbers and stories around Jev are “shocking.” Almost everyone seems to be trying it. He thinks the product is strong, but the moment also matters. Many builders feel AI is too expensive or too slow. So they are hungry for tools that let them put AI in more places. Vercel even made Jev free on its platform for the weekend.

Box CEO Aaron Levie showed why enterprises might care. In a Box demo, Jev pulled an incident report, asked whether it was customer-facing and how severe it was, moved the file into escalate, monitor, or review folders, and wrote metadata with the result. All of that happened almost instantly and at almost no cost. Levie said this kind of split-second judgment — a quick decision in a workflow — can help with insurance claims, contracts, loan processing, and security reviews. FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari added a playful proof: Jev scored 3,000 kids’ snacks with several criteria in 28 seconds for about $0.11. He also built Jevable, a site that collects fun Jev demos from X.

Rauch had a second chart worth noticing. On Vercel’s AI Gateway, open models took about 78.4% of token volume that day, versus 21.6% for closed models. Spend told a different story, but Moonshot AI and DeepSeek still ranked high, and with Z.ai their combined spend passed OpenAI in that snapshot. He was careful: this is inference spend across providers, mostly in the US, not cash paid straight to open-weight labs. Still, it shows how hard the market is pushing for cheaper, open options.

OpenAI also teed up a busy week ahead. Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT, said he spent the day on a keynote with Romain Huet and Sam Altman. The hard part was not building the features. It was explaining “so much good stuff” in a short talk. Some pieces will ship next week so people do not wait for everything at once.

Outside the big labs, personal agents kept looking more useful in daily life. AI tutor Peter Yang called Meta’s Muse the best personal agent he has tried. It helped him save over $800 a year on cable and phone bills. In one call, Muse negotiated another $288 in annual Comcast savings. His blunt line: most company support phone lines are not ready for agents yet.

Put together, the day sat next to two pressures. One is shared rules for coding agents, such as AGENTS.md. The other is the volume of demand for faster, cheaper model calls — from free Jev weekends to open-model traffic on gateways. The models keep getting stronger. The winning products are the ones that make those models follow your rules and fit your latency budget.

Sentence Focus

Starting today in version 2.1.277, if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md.
- Starting today in version 2.1.277, / if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, / Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md.
- “if there is no …” 是条件从句；主句用 “will check for and use” 表示找到就用。
- 从今天起，在 2.1.277 版本里，如果文件夹里没有 CLAUDE.md，Claude 就会查找并使用 AGENTS.md。

He thinks the product is strong, but this is also downstream of the “AI is too expensive/slow” zeitgeist.
- He thinks the product is strong, / but this is also downstream of / the “AI is too expensive/slow” zeitgeist.
- “downstream of” 表示「处在……之后、被其推动」；zeitgeist 指时代情绪/风气。
- 他认为产品本身很强，但这股热潮也处在「AI 太贵/太慢」这股时代情绪的下游。

That kind of split-second judgment sits next to the volume of demand for cheaper model calls.
- That kind of split-second judgment / sits next to / the volume of demand / for cheaper model calls.
- “sits next to” 表示两件事并排放在一起、形成对照；“volume of” 指体量，不是音量。
- 这种分秒级判断，就挨着对更便宜模型调用的巨大需求。

item.content:encoded:
Title for RSS: Claude Projects, family agents, and a flood of tiny software

The main story in today’s AI builder feed is simple. Anthropic is rolling out Claude Projects. The idea is not “one more chat.” It is a shared workspace that remembers how you work.

Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said Projects changed how he talks to Claude and how he writes code. He stopped managing many separate sessions. He now sends thoughts as they come. Claude splits them into threads. The project remembers his habits. That is where he does much of his coding now. Cat Wu, who works on Claude Code and Cowork, described the same shift. Claude coordinates all of her sessions. She can fire off a batch of tasks and move on. Claude keeps context on her work, can give a status update when she asks, and has long-lived memory that evolves with use. The rollout continues over the coming weeks.

Claude Code’s Thariq added the architecture view. Projects brings the design of Claude Tag into Claude Code. There is one agent per project. That agent manages memory and spins off subagents for tasks. You can ask it to be proactive, or to do things on a schedule. In his words, it feels nicer than a bunch of sessions.

The official Claude account filled in limits and promises. A project builds over time. Every thread adds to and draws from shared memory, such as a release moving to Friday, or who to ask before touching billing. The project library keeps files you add and files Claude creates. Threads run in the cloud, so they keep working even if your computer is offline. Local files and internal networks are not reachable yet. Local support is coming soon. Existing projects on Pro and Max keep working for now, and Anthropic will upgrade them as the rollout expands.

Outside coding tools, Google Labs announced a family-focused CC — an AI agent so families spend less time on logistics and more time together. You can add up to five members. Mornings can start with a shared “Your Day Ahead” brief email. Schedules and to-dos can autosync with a shared Google Calendar and Tasks. Families can coordinate in Google Chat with CC for jobs such as weekly meal plans. The waitlist is for the US, ages 18+. Google’s Josh Woodward said his own family likes it.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch pushed a different scale story. Vercel took 10 years to reach 1 billion deployments. Then it added another 1.4 billion in the last 10 months alone. He thinks more software may be produced next year than in all of computing history so far — from tiny personal tools to full apps, agents, and platforms. The company says it can deploy, upload, assign a domain, and globally propagate an artifact in about one second. For urgent hotfixes, agents can now run `vercel --turbo --prod` on the fastest build machine.

Box CEO Aaron Levie looked at the same world from the inference side. He said agents already make up the majority of inference, and over the next year or two that share may trend toward nearly all inference. Most tokens, in his view, will be spent by agents that run tasks in the background around the clock. Just in the past week, he said, he introduced multiple new workflows that were not technically possible even a month ago.

Two smaller notes sit next to these moves. YC’s Garry Tan highlighted Memorable, which optimizes memory with embeddings instead of more tokens. FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari shared nosugarforkids.com, a healthy-snack catalog for kids built with Claude in the loop. A daily Claude agent updates the catalog, checks search performance, and writes content. With zero backlinks and no social presence, he said the site still grew to about 6,000 impressions and 60 clicks a day.

Put together, the day was about shared memory and background work. Claude Projects wants one agent to hold a whole project. Google’s family CC wants one agent to hold a household calendar. Vercel is racing to ship tiny software at scale. Levie is betting agents will soon use almost all of the tokens. The question is no longer only “how smart is the model?” It is “who keeps the memory, and who keeps working when you walk away?”

Sentence Focus

He stopped managing many separate sessions.
- He stopped managing / many separate sessions.
- “stopped + -ing” 表示停下某件一直在做的事；“many separate sessions” 强调以前要自己管很多分散会话。
- 他不再自己管理许多彼此分开的会话。

Threads run in the cloud, so they keep working even if your computer is offline.
- Threads run in the cloud, / so they keep working / even if your computer is offline.
- “even if …” 是让步：就算电脑离线，线程仍继续跑；“so” 连接原因与结果。
- 线程跑在云端，所以即便你的电脑离线，它们也继续工作。

That kind of shared memory sits next to the volume of tiny software now being deployed.
- That kind of shared memory / sits next to / the volume of tiny software / now being deployed.
- “sits next to” 表示两件事并排放在一起、形成对照；“volume of” 指体量/数量，不是声音大小。
- 这种共享记忆，就挨着眼下正在大量部署的微型软件。

item.content:encoded:
Title for RSS: One Claude for chat and real work

Anthropic’s big product move this week is simple to say. Claude Cowork and chat are becoming one Claude. You no longer have to decide which “door” to open for a task.

For a long time, chat was for quick questions. Cowork was for bigger jobs, such as reports and files. Design was for visuals. Many people used all of them. But they also got tired of choosing. Work started in one place often did not carry into another. So Anthropic stopped making you choose. Claude can now look at your prompt and decide what the task needs: a fast answer, deeper agent work (software that can take steps for you), or a document, a slide deck, or a design. Claude Code’s Cat Wu said users keep control. You can still stop, change direction, or ask for more or less effort.

Claude Code’s Boris Cherny framed the story as one long path. Claude Code showed that AI can do real work, not only answer questions. Developers hand Claude a feature and come back to shipped code. Cowork showed the same idea for knowledge work: hand over a brief and come back to finished files. The next step, he said, is one Claude that keeps context across everything you are doing, wherever you are. He has used the merged experience for weeks and called it simpler, faster, and more powerful. The rollout will be slow so the team can keep it reliable.

The same update brings Claude Docs, Claude Slides, and Claude Design into the conversation. Ask for a presentation and you get one you can open, edit, and export as PowerPoint or PDF. Anthropic Research’s Alex Albert said the merged UX feels better than chat or Cowork alone. Every CEO Dan Shipper put it more loudly: the “tabs era” is ending.

The official Claude blog walked through a concrete day. A weekly report is due at noon. Before you leave, you ask Claude what moved in the pipeline, then add: write it the usual way, flag anything that slipped, and put the highlights in five slides. You can check progress on your phone. By the time you reach your desk, the report and the slides are waiting — and they already match because they came from the same chat. By default, Claude asks before it acts. The change rolls out first to Pro and Max, then Team and Free. One quote from Senior Economist Andrew Keller captured the hope: Claude could open a legal research database, pull cases, read them, find related cases, download them, and store them for human review.

Not every voice was only praise. Builder Zara Zhang said she uses Claude less because its way of speaking feels exhausting — as if it is always trying to look smart instead of making a clear point. That kind of blunt feedback sits next to the launch excitement.

Outside Anthropic, the feed had other sharp notes. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the main thing he wanted to launch this week will slip to next week, but he thinks it is worth the wait. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux quoted that delay with a dry line: sometimes physics can’t be cheated. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said typesafeai’s fx tool runs in auto by default, with a safety reviewer on every command. That reviewer runs on GPT Luna today. Jev, he said, is up to about 18× faster at p95 and more accurate, and it is coming to Vercel’s AI Gateway. Claude Code’s Thariq said bash is no longer “all you need” for reliable tool calling, though sandboxes plus bash still help for code generation and execution. Box CEO Aaron Levie pointed to another open space: models that are very fast and cheap, yet still capable, for enterprise tasks such as classification and routing.

Put together, the day was less about a new model name and more about product shape. Anthropic is betting that one Claude, with docs and slides inside the chat, will remove the friction of tabs. OpenAI is asking people to wait one more week. And builders keep arguing about voice, tools, and speed — the parts that decide whether strong models feel useful at work.

Sentence Focus

Claude can now look at your prompt and decide what the task needs: a fast answer, deeper agent work, or a document, a slide deck, or a design.
- Claude can now look at your prompt / and decide what the task needs: / a fast answer, / deeper agent work, / or a document, a slide deck, or a design.
- “decide what the task needs” 后用冒号列出选项；“or A, B, or C” 是并列选择。
- Claude 现在能看你的提示，并判断任务需要什么：快速回答、更深的 agent 工作，或文档、幻灯片或设计。

By the time you reach your desk, the report and the slides are waiting — and they already match because they came from the same chat.
- By the time you reach your desk, / the report and the slides are waiting / — and they already match / because they came from the same chat.
- “By the time …” 表示「到……的时候」；破折号后补原因，because 从句说明为何已经一致。
- 等你到办公桌时，报告和幻灯片已经在等你——而且它们已经对齐，因为来自同一次对话。

That kind of blunt feedback sits next to the launch excitement.
- That kind of blunt feedback / sits next to / the launch excitement.
- “blunt” 指直白、不绕弯；“sits next to” 表示两种东西并排出现、形成对照，不是字面「坐在旁边」。
- 这种直白的反馈，就挨着发布时的兴奋声。

item.title: Models are strong — the hard part is still the bridge to work
item.description:
Title for RSS: Models are strong — the hard part is still the bridge to work

Today’s AI news kept coming back to one idea. The models are powerful. The hard part is still connecting that power to real company work.
item.content:encoded:
Title for RSS: Models are strong — the hard part is still the bridge to work

Today’s AI news kept coming back to one idea. The models are powerful. The hard part is still connecting that power to real company work.

Box CEO Aaron Levie put this in plain words on Training Data and again on X. He said there is a big gap between what models can do and the workflows enterprises want to automate. That gap, he argued, is the chance for an “applied AI” layer — software that sits next to the model and makes it useful at work. In his view, you need to link intelligence to workflows, rebuild some processes, pull the right context and data, keep people in the loop, run change management, do domain-specific evals (tests that check quality in a real field), and manage security. Even if models keep getting better, this layer still matters. Stronger models let you try harder tasks, so the bridge can become even more important.

Levie also talked about “diffusion” — how AI spreads through many companies, not only through a few big labs. A chatbot can be general. A real workflow often needs something else. It may need to ping you at the right step. It may need data the chatbot cannot reach on its own. Someone still has to set that up inside the company and add domain knowledge. Unless the big labs hire something like 100,000 people to do all of that, he said, a large “diffusion economy” will grow: teams that help firms of every size change how they work. One memorable line from the talk was simple: “You’re either a year ahead or a year behind simply based on your feed.”

On the product side, Claude moved deeper into day-to-day business tools. Salesforce in Claude is now in beta. It brings accounts, opportunities, and pipeline into Claude, with 37 pre-built sales skills. You can prep a call, review a deal, build a pipeline dashboard, or send a forecast without leaving the chat. Separately, Claude for Small Business added more ready workflows and 27 new integrations with tools owners already use, such as Shopify, Salesforce, Stripe, and Zapier. The product has been installed more than 900,000 times since May. After listening to owners on a spring tour, Anthropic said about a third wanted help growing the business — leads, inbound questions, and proposals — not only running the back office.

Elsewhere, builders argued about how models should judge and connect. Every CEO Dan Shipper said his team almost never tests new foundation models, but one recent model felt different. It does not mainly output words. It outputs probabilities. In their testing, it could act as a judge in places where you might need a much larger model, yet it was about 25× faster and about 600× cheaper. Replit CEO Amjad Masad pushed back on the wider trend: if you already know the set of possible answers, why not train a model to score those options directly with logprobs (probability scores over a fixed list)? Claude Code’s Thariq said another integration bet is shifting too. He now thinks MCP is better than CLIs for most integrations, because tool calling is stronger, tools can be deferred, and MCP is stateless.

Infrastructure voices kept the same theme: give people choice, and show your work. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch formally introduced Vercel Labs as a public home for research and experiments. He also said the future is multi-model. Hiding the choice, in his view, confuses customers and keeps them from learning which tool fits the job. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman teased a heavy shipping week before DevDay. YC’s Garry Tan said Capy plus his GStack/GBrain setup cut a day of fix work to about half, using the same frontier models.

Put together, the day was less about a brand-new model name and more about the messy middle. Levie’s bridge, Claude’s sales and small-business connectors, probability judges, MCP tools, and multi-model product design all point to the same problem: intelligence is not enough until it sits next to real workflows, real data, and real people.

Sentence Focus

That gap, he argued, is the chance for an “applied AI” layer — software that sits next to the model and makes it useful at work.
- That gap, / he argued, / is the chance for an “applied AI” layer / — software that sits next to the model / and makes it useful at work.
- “he argued” 插入语；“sits next to” 表示紧挨着、配合使用，不是字面「坐在旁边」。
- 他认为，那道鸿沟正是「应用层 AI」的机会：一类紧挨着模型、让它在工作中真正有用的软件。

Even if models keep getting better, this layer still matters.
- Even if models keep getting better, / this layer still matters.
- “Even if …” 让步：就算模型继续变强，后面结论仍成立。
- 即便模型不断变强，这一层仍然重要。

Unless the big labs hire something like 100,000 people to do all of that, he said, a large “diffusion economy” will grow.
- Unless the big labs hire something like 100,000 people to do all of that, / he said, / a large “diffusion economy” will grow.
- “Unless …” = 「除非…否则」；主句在逗号后，说明扩散经济会出现的条件。
- 他说，除非大实验室雇差不多十万人去包办这一切，否则会成长出很大的「扩散经济」。

item.title: Agents will do 100× more work — if we can contain them
item.description:
Agents are no longer a side feature. Over the past day, builders and labs described a world in which agents run in the background, touch more systems than people ever did, and need new security, compute, and product surfaces to keep up.

Box CEO Aaron Levie pushed that shift into plain numbers. Agent swarms, better computer use, the next wave of APIs and MCP servers, and new form factors such as Muse or Instinct will sit next to vertical enterprise agents and background workflow agents. Together, they will throw agents at far more professional and personal tasks than a single chat session can hold — recruiting talent, watching customer signals, mining transcripts, reviewing code, and brute-force testing systems. Levie’s claim is blunt: the volume of work agents will do may be about 100 times what people first imagined, while the industry is still roughly 1% of the way into how those agents are shaped, deployed, managed, and budgeted.

That scale creates a second problem that is harder than raw capability. When agents use enterprise systems 100 times more often than humans ever did, protecting data becomes one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the century. Security and productivity are locked together. Give an agent too much open access, and control becomes weak; lock everything down, and you get almost no AI gain. As one example, Box Shield can now set granular controls on what content agents may touch based on document classification, plus alerts for unusual agent access.

Anthropic made a similar point from the lab side. In “How we contain Claude across products,” the company wrote that access strong enough to take down an internal Anthropic service would have been rejected a year ago; today that level of access is routine because developers are more productive with it. Risk has two parts: how likely a failure is, and how large the blast radius would be. Human-in-the-loop approval sounds safe, but telemetry showed users approved about 93% of permission prompts, and approval fatigue makes people less careful over time. Anthropic’s main bet is containment — sandboxes, virtual machines, and egress controls that limit what an agent is able to do. The post also noted that Claude Mythos Preview’s blast radius was judged too high for a broad April 2026 release.

A second Anthropic post explained why some Claude Code users recently felt the product had gotten worse. Three separate product-layer changes, not the API, stacked on different traffic slices and looked like broad degradation: a default reasoning-effort cut from high to medium that was later reversed; a caching bug that cleared old thinking every turn instead of once after idle time; and a verbosity prompt that hurt coding quality. By April 23, Anthropic said all three were fixed as of v2.1.116 and that usage limits would be reset for all subscribers.

While repairing quality, Anthropic also described how long-running agents should scale. In “Scaling Managed Agents,” the team argued that harnesses encode assumptions that go stale as models improve. Their answer is to virtualize an agent the way operating systems virtualized hardware: a session as an append-only log, a harness as the loop that calls Claude and routes tools, and a sandbox as the place where code and files live. Early designs put everything in one container and accidentally adopted a “pet” server that was hard to debug and hard to connect to a customer’s private cloud. Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” lets the harness treat the container like any other tool call, rebuild it when it dies, and keep interfaces stable while implementations change. On the product surface, Claude Code can now turn session work into live artifacts — PR walkthroughs, dashboards, and release checklists that update in place and stay private to an organization unless shared.

Outside Anthropic, shipping stories moved in the same direction. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux said this week’s releases could match the density people expected from DevDay 2025, while asking which Codex features should be deleted. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch welcomed Steren, the creator of Google Cloud Run, to lead Vercel’s Fluid compute family, arguing that serverless was the last chapter of the cloud and that agents need new compute primitives. Rauch also said agents are only as good as the proof-checkers, compilers, type systems, and linters you give them. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny reported that Claude Mods are landing, with community demos already including Tetris inside Claude.

Taken together, the day had one shape. Builders are raising their estimate of how much work agents will do. Labs are writing down how to contain that work, how to recover when product changes quietly hurt quality, and how to host long-horizon agents without treating every container as a fragile pet. The product layer is already racing to match the load Levie described.

Sentence Focus

When agents use enterprise systems 100 times more often than humans ever did, protecting data becomes one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the century.
- When agents use enterprise systems / 100 times more often than humans ever did, / protecting data becomes / one of the more complex security and governance challenges / of the century.
- “100 times more often than …” 是频率比较；“protecting data becomes …” 用动名词短语作主语，把“保护数据”整件事当成一个抽象问题。
- 当 agent 使用企业系统的频率达到人类以往的 100 倍时，保护数据会成为本世纪更复杂的安全与治理挑战之一。

Risk has two parts: how likely a failure is, and how large the blast radius would be.
- Risk has two parts: / how likely a failure is, / and how large the blast radius would be.
- 冒号后用两个 how 从句并列解释 “two parts”；“blast radius” 是爆炸半径的隐喻，指一次失败可能波及的范围。
- 风险有两部分：失败有多可能发生，以及爆炸半径会有多大。

Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” lets the harness treat the container like any other tool call, rebuild it when it dies, and keep interfaces stable while implementations change.
- Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” / lets the harness / treat the container like any other tool call, / rebuild it when it dies, / and keep interfaces stable / while implementations change.
- “Decoupling … lets …” 动名词作主语；后面三个不带 to 的动词并列（treat / rebuild / keep）；“while implementations change” 表示实现在变、接口仍稳。
- 把「脑」与「手」解耦，能让 harness 像对待其他工具调用一样对待容器，在它挂掉时重建，并在实现不断变化时保持接口稳定。

Box CEO Aaron Levie pushed that shift into plain numbers. Agent swarms, better computer use, the next wave of APIs and MCP servers, and new form factors such as Muse or Instinct will sit next to vertical enterprise agents and background workflow agents. Together, they will throw agents at far more professional and personal tasks than a single chat session can hold — recruiting talent, watching customer signals, mining transcripts, reviewing code, and brute-force testing systems. Levie’s claim is blunt: the volume of work agents will do may be about 100 times what people first imagined, while the industry is still roughly 1% of the way into how those agents are shaped, deployed, managed, and budgeted.

That scale creates a second problem that is harder than raw capability. When agents use enterprise systems 100 times more often than humans ever did, protecting data becomes one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the century. Security and productivity are locked together. Give an agent too much open access, and control becomes weak; lock everything down, and you get almost no AI gain. As one example, Box Shield can now set granular controls on what content agents may touch based on document classification, plus alerts for unusual agent access.

Anthropic made a similar point from the lab side. In “How we contain Claude across products,” the company wrote that access strong enough to take down an internal Anthropic service would have been rejected a year ago; today that level of access is routine because developers are more productive with it. Risk has two parts: how likely a failure is, and how large the blast radius would be. Human-in-the-loop approval sounds safe, but telemetry showed users approved about 93% of permission prompts, and approval fatigue makes people less careful over time. Anthropic’s main bet is containment — sandboxes, virtual machines, and egress controls that limit what an agent is able to do. The post also noted that Claude Mythos Preview’s blast radius was judged too high for a broad April 2026 release.

A second Anthropic post explained why some Claude Code users recently felt the product had gotten worse. Three separate product-layer changes, not the API, stacked on different traffic slices and looked like broad degradation: a default reasoning-effort cut from high to medium that was later reversed; a caching bug that cleared old thinking every turn instead of once after idle time; and a verbosity prompt that hurt coding quality. By April 23, Anthropic said all three were fixed as of v2.1.116 and that usage limits would be reset for all subscribers.

While repairing quality, Anthropic also described how long-running agents should scale. In “Scaling Managed Agents,” the team argued that harnesses encode assumptions that go stale as models improve. Their answer is to virtualize an agent the way operating systems virtualized hardware: a session as an append-only log, a harness as the loop that calls Claude and routes tools, and a sandbox as the place where code and files live. Early designs put everything in one container and accidentally adopted a “pet” server that was hard to debug and hard to connect to a customer’s private cloud. Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” lets the harness treat the container like any other tool call, rebuild it when it dies, and keep interfaces stable while implementations change. On the product surface, Claude Code can now turn session work into live artifacts — PR walkthroughs, dashboards, and release checklists that update in place and stay private to an organization unless shared.

Outside Anthropic, shipping stories moved in the same direction. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux said this week’s releases could match the density people expected from DevDay 2025, while asking which Codex features should be deleted. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch welcomed Steren, the creator of Google Cloud Run, to lead Vercel’s Fluid compute family, arguing that serverless was the last chapter of the cloud and that agents need new compute primitives. Rauch also said agents are only as good as the proof-checkers, compilers, type systems, and linters you give them. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny reported that Claude Mods are landing, with community demos already including Tetris inside Claude.

Taken together, the day had one shape. Builders are raising their estimate of how much work agents will do. Labs are writing down how to contain that work, how to recover when product changes quietly hurt quality, and how to host long-horizon agents without treating every container as a fragile pet. The product layer is already racing to match the load Levie described.

Sentence Focus

When agents use enterprise systems 100 times more often than humans ever did, protecting data becomes one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the century.
- When agents use enterprise systems / 100 times more often than humans ever did, / protecting data becomes / one of the more complex security and governance challenges / of the century.
- “100 times more often than …” 是频率比较；“protecting data becomes …” 用动名词短语作主语，把“保护数据”整件事当成一个抽象问题。
- 当 agent 使用企业系统的频率达到人类以往的 100 倍时，保护数据会成为本世纪更复杂的安全与治理挑战之一。

Risk has two parts: how likely a failure is, and how large the blast radius would be.
- Risk has two parts: / how likely a failure is, / and how large the blast radius would be.
- 冒号后用两个 how 从句并列解释 “two parts”；“blast radius” 是爆炸半径的隐喻，指一次失败可能波及的范围。
- 风险有两部分：失败有多可能发生，以及爆炸半径会有多大。

Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” lets the harness treat the container like any other tool call, rebuild it when it dies, and keep interfaces stable while implementations change.
- Decoupling the “brain” from the “hands” / lets the harness / treat the container like any other tool call, / rebuild it when it dies, / and keep interfaces stable / while implementations change.
- “Decoupling … lets …” 动名词作主语；后面三个不带 to 的动词并列（treat / rebuild / keep）；“while implementations change” 表示实现在变、接口仍稳。
- 把「脑」与「手」解耦，能让 harness 像对待其他工具调用一样对待容器，在它挂掉时重建，并在实现不断变化时保持接口稳定。

item.title: Sam Altman doubles down on pacing — while builders remind us most of the world is still early
item.description:
Frontier AI leaders spent the day arguing about speed, safety, and who is actually using these tools. The loudest thread came from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who tried to make the word “pacing” less political and more operational. In his telling, pacing does not mean stopping. It means keeping alignment, monitoring, and safety work ahead of raw model capability, even when that choice has a real cost.

Altman said the public deserves confidence that American companies building frontier systems will act responsibly, especially as progress has steepened. He welcomed a federal framework with consistent safety requirements, but argued labs should not wait for an antitrust exemption or new legislation before starting. Years ago, companies wrote Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks that focused mainly on releasing finished models. Today’s shift, he said, is toward safer development itself. At OpenAI, teams now prepare explicit safety cases before frontier reinforcement-learning runs that are expected to raise capability a lot — not only before a public launch.

He also named two futures he wants the industry to avoid. The first is losing control of the future to AI; OpenAI, he wrote, is unapologetically on “Team Humanity.” The second is extreme concentration of power, where one person, company, country, or lab uses extraordinarily powerful AI to press one worldview onto everyone else. Walking between those threats, he argued, requires shared standards on misalignment, monitoring, and safety, plus international coordination that governments must help with later.

Box CEO Aaron Levie added a careful middle voice. He admitted that “pacing” can sound like an arbitrary slowdown or a regulatory tool that hobbles rivals. Even so, he said the concrete improvement goals in Dario Amodei’s recent writing are necessities, not slogans. AI will sit under trading systems, medical devices, biotech breakthroughs, defense tools, and government workflows. In those domains, people already expect safety and alignment. The hard problem of the century, Levie wrote, is how to get there without meaningfully slowing innovation or reducing competition.

While that governance debate ran hot, AI educator Peter Yang pulled attention back to adoption. Quoting Brex CEO Pedro and a February 2026 chart, Yang noted that most of the world has barely started. In the chart, each dot stood for about 3.2 million people. Gray boxes — never used AI — were about 84%. Green boxes — free chatbot users — were about 16%. Orange boxes — people paying roughly $20 a month — were about 0.3%. The tiny red box of people using agents effectively was about 0.04%. Even if usage has risen since February, Yang’s point was simple: the industry is still early, and public fear often races ahead of real penetration.

Product builders meanwhile kept shipping the agent layer that sits inside that tiny red box. Replit CEO Amjad Masad said it had been painful to watch users get priced out of AI coding; now, he claimed, it is free to build again. OpenClaw builder Peter Steinberger reported that the next release (or the dev channel) makes worktrees roughly 80% faster through folder clones on APFS, btrfs, xfs, and ReFS, while saving disk space. The stack is written in Rust. He plans to test for a few weeks and, if it helps most users, try to push the idea into Codex. Builder Zara Zhang highlighted a different agent pain: Astra may agree that it should do Y after a correction, yet fail to actually do Y — unlike other models that simply continue. Every CEO Dan Shipper joked that he started using Astra medium for simple tasks and called it “pacing the frontier.”

Away from models, FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari warned founders’ recruits that a higher entry valuation and higher total compensation are often a bug, not a feature. A company that raised at a richer price is not automatically safer. Candidates should look at market, traction, positioning, a realistic exit, and 409A tax effects. He spoke from experience: he once joined a company that raised $60 million from top-tier investors and still folded within three years, wiping out equity.

Taken together, the day had one clear shape. Lab leaders are trying to define pacing as disciplined development rather than a stop sign. Enterprise and infrastructure builders still insist safety goals are real for mission-critical systems. At the same time, the adoption chart and the agent product notes tell a quieter story: only a thin slice of people use agents well, and that slice is already arguing about pricing, worktree speed, and whether the model will act after it says “you’re right.”

Sentence Focus

1. In his telling, pacing does not mean stopping.
- In his telling, / pacing does not mean stopping.
- “In his telling” = “按他的说法 / 在他的叙述里”，用 telling 指整套说法，而不是字面“告诉”。
- 按他的说法，放慢节奏并不等于停下来。

2. Even so, he said the concrete improvement goals in Dario Amodei’s recent writing are necessities, not slogans.
- Even so, / he said / the concrete improvement goals / in Dario Amodei’s recent writing / are necessities, / not slogans.
- “Even so” 承接上句让步；“necessities, not slogans” 是对照名词短语，强调“硬需求 vs 口号”。
- 即便如此，他说 Dario Amodei 近期文章里那些具体改进目标是硬需求，而不是口号。

3. Even if usage has risen since February, Yang’s point was simple: the industry is still early, and public fear often races ahead of real penetration.
- Even if usage has risen since February, / Yang’s point was simple: / the industry is still early, / and public fear often races ahead of real penetration.
- “Even if …” 让步从句；“races ahead of” 把抽象名词 fear / penetration 写成赛跑，表示恐惧跑在真实渗透率前面。
- 即便 2 月以来使用量已经上升，Yang 的观点仍然很简单：行业还很早期，而公众恐惧常常跑在真实渗透率前面。

item.title: Industry voices push for slower frontier AI — and for outside eyes inside the labs
item.description:
Over the past day, a clear theme ran through posts from people who build and ship frontier AI: move carefully, harden systems, and let independent experts look deeper into the labs.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he agrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to slow the pace at the frontier. Altman framed this as more than a polite nod. He said the topic has been a core issue inside OpenAI for the past few weeks. He also backed a practical idea that is gaining attention: give independent evaluators access similar to that of employees inside frontier AI laboratories. In plain terms, outsiders would not only read public papers. They would get closer to the tools, logs, and internal views that staff already see. Altman promised that OpenAI would take this path as well, with more details still to come.

That proposal sounds unusual in consumer tech, but several builders argued it is normal in other high-risk fields. Anthropic researcher Alex Albert pointed out that banks already host federal examiners, and nuclear plants keep full-time on-site inspectors. In his view, putting “embedded evaluators” into frontier labs is a first step that is both serious and realistic. Meta AI senior director Madhu Guru went further on the talent side. He predicted that over the next twelve months, more top people will leave a small set of labs, data firms, and independent research groups for places like METR, which focus on evaluating frontier models. He said funding, financial independence from lab equity, and a rising sense of existential risk will push that shift. Even when he does not fully agree with Dario’s essay, Guru still urged people to read it carefully and to seek shared language on opportunity, risk, second-order effects, and cross-border coordination.

Not everyone treated “slow down” as a soft slogan. Anthropic’s Thariq, who works on Claude Code, wrote that if someone in 2018 had seen today’s Claude Code, they might have called it AGI. Software engineering and society have absorbed huge change, he said, yet cracks are starting to show. Many AI practitioners feel tired but keep pushing. His request was simple: leave room for system hardening and for public debate. He said his own p(doom) is not high, but resilience comes from making hard decisions together. Replit CEO Amjad Masad echoed the same mood, especially around security. Slowing down to harden systems matters, he argued, because the industry has not yet found every system that recent agents have broken into.

Box CEO Aaron Levie struck a careful middle tone. He did not claim to agree with every line of Dario’s piece, but he said it captured many real constraints on how frontier AI can move. At this capability level, some form of coordinated self-discipline is almost unavoidable. The hard part, Levie said, is agreeing on the rules — and whether politics still leaves labs space to speak. An even larger question is whether countries join in. Any slowdown depends on wide participation, and game theory makes that unlikely until risks look more obvious. Expect more mess, he warned.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch added a different layer. On the builder side, he said teams now iterate in Zig, Go, and Rust as fast as in TypeScript or Python. Language choice is less about human comfort; agents are becoming a new kind of compiler that turns intent into high-speed software. His harness can already orchestrate sub-agents with different models and reasoning effort — for example, one model planning while another executes — through AGENTS.md or a prompt, with humans able to interrupt and steer. On policy, Rauch accepted that AI safety and cybersecurity worries are fair, but he warned against talking the United States into self-limits and heavy bureaucracy. He also pushed back on one popular talking point: treating “OpenAI hacking Hugging Face” as a clean argument for embedded evaluators. In ExploitGym-style settings, he said, agents are meant to exploit systems, and rivals will not slow down just because evaluators sit inside US labs.

Away from the governance debate, Anthropic also shipped product news that shows how agents are moving into daily workflows. Claude in Chrome is now generally available for paid Claude plans. The agent can navigate, read, click, and fill forms in the browser, reusing logins you already have, while a safety classifier checks actions before they run. The company highlighted defenses against prompt injection, including attack-library training, probes on tool results, and automatic approval that checks whether an action still matches the user’s original intent. In stronger red-team tests, attack success fell sharply once probes and classifiers were added for newer models. Separately, Claude Cowork on desktop now includes Claude’s own built-in browser: a side panel that Claude controls, without seeing your other tabs, bookmarks, or passwords by default. Users can import selected site logins from Chrome, Edge, or Firefox, while banks, email, and SSO stay out unless the user actively includes them.

Taken together, the day’s signals point in one direction. Product builders keep putting agents into browsers, harnesses, and enterprise files. At the same time, leaders across OpenAI, Anthropic’s circle, Meta AI, Replit, Box, and Vercel are arguing — sometimes from opposite angles — about how fast the frontier should move, who gets to look inside, and how to harden systems before the next wave of agent-driven risk arrives.

Sentence Focus

1. He also backed a practical idea that is gaining attention: give independent evaluators access similar to that of employees inside frontier AI laboratories. 2. Even when he does not fully agree with Dario’s essay, Guru still urged people to read it carefully and to seek shared language on opportunity, risk, second-order effects, and cross-border coordination. 3. Any slowdown depends on wide participation, and game theory makes that unlikely until risks look more obvious.
